html:
Driglam namzha is Bhutan's official code of dress and conduct, rooted in the rules of the Zhabdrung in the 17th century and made compulsory for all citizens by a royal decree of 1989.

It requires the national dress, the gho for men and the kira for women, in schools, offices and dzongs, and sets the forms of greeting, sitting and speaking before officials. It is meant to protect the Drukpa Buddhist culture of a small state wedged between India and China.

In the south, the Nepali-speaking Lhotshampa saw the decree, with new citizenship rules and an end to Nepali teaching, as an attack on them. Protests in 1990 were put down, and about a hundred thousand left or were driven out, becoming the Bhutanese refugees in camps in Nepal. Most were later resettled in the United States and other countries.
sum: Driglam namzha is Bhutan's official code of dress and conduct, rooted in the rules of the Zhabdrung in the 17th century and made compulsory for all citizens by a royal decree of 1989.
